parts.title: A different route home
parts.instructions: Read the story and choose the best answer.
parts.passage:
During my first summer working in Scotland, I stayed in a small village near the hills. One Saturday, I planned to take a bus to the coast. The driver told me that roadworks had stopped the service, but a local woman said there was another way. She pointed to a path behind the old church.

I followed it through a forest and past a stream. The walk was longer than I expected, so I began to worry that I had taken a wrong turn. Then I heard music. A family was having a picnic beside a small lake, and they showed me where the path joined the main road.

I reached the coast in time to watch the sun go down. I never did take that bus, but I discovered a beautiful place I would not have seen otherwise. When I visit again, I plan to walk the same route with a friend.

questions.prompt: Why couldn’t the writer take the bus?
options: The bus was too full to get on
The writer arrived after it had left
questions.explanation: The driver said roadworks had stopped the bus service.

questions.prompt: Who suggested another route?
questions.explanation: A local woman said there was another way and pointed to a path.

questions.prompt: Why did the writer become worried?
options: The weather was getting colder and wetter
The walk was taking longer than expected
The path was too crowded with walkers
questions.explanation: The walk was longer than she expected, so she worried she had taken a wrong turn.

questions.prompt: How did the family help?
options: They drove the writer to the coast
They lent the writer a map
They showed where to find the road
They gave the writer some food
questions.explanation: The family showed her where the path joined the main road.

questions.prompt: What does the writer plan to do next time?
options: Take an earlier bus to the coast
Stay near the lake for longer
questions.explanation: She plans to walk the same route with a friend when she visits again.

parts.title: A weekend on an island
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There are three extra sentences.
parts.passage:
My friends and I booked a weekend on a small island. We expected to spend most of the time on the beach. [1] The owner lent us bicycles, so we decided to explore.

Our first stop was a lighthouse at the north end. [2] The view from the top was worth the climb.

After lunch, we followed a path through a village. [3] She told us that the local market opened early on Sundays.

We set our alarms for the next morning. [4] We bought fresh bread and fruit for the journey home.

The weekend went quickly, but we came back with plenty of stories. [5] I would recommend the island to anyone who enjoys walking.
sentences: But when we arrived, the sky was grey and it was too cold to swim.
A woman at a small shop gave us a useful tip.
A ferry runs between the island and the mainland every hour.
We got up at seven and visited the market.
It was a short trip, but I felt fully relaxed afterwards.
A steep staircase led to the top.
Many of the houses had red doors and small gardens.
The streets were almost empty at that time.

gaps.explanation: The grey, cold weather explains why they did not stay on the beach, and leads to “The owner lent us bicycles, so we decided to explore”.
“A steep staircase led to the top” follows the lighthouse and leads to “The view from the top”.
“A woman at a small shop gave us a useful tip” introduces “She told us” about the market.
“We got up at seven and visited the market” follows setting the alarms and leads to buying bread and fruit.
“It was a short trip, but I felt fully relaxed afterwards” follows the weekend going quickly and leads to the recommendation.

parts.title: Getting ready to travel
parts.instructions: Choose the correct word for each gap.
parts.passage: Before a long journey, I always make a [1] of the things I need. I check the weather so I can choose the right [2]. I also keep my passport in a safe [3] in my bag. If I arrive early, I like to [4] a little time looking around the station. It’s important to leave home [5] enough to avoid rushing. That way, the trip can start in a [6] mood.

questions.prompt: Gap 1
questions.explanation: A list is a set of things written down that you need to take.

questions.prompt: Gap 2
questions.explanation: You choose clothes to suit the weather; costumes and uniforms are for special purposes.

questions.prompt: Gap 3
questions.explanation: A safe place is a spot where something will not be lost.

questions.prompt: Gap 4
questions.explanation: You spend time doing something; cost, pay and lend do not take “time looking around”.

questions.prompt: Gap 5
questions.explanation: “Early enough” means in good time; the other words do not combine with “enough” here.

questions.prompt: Gap 6
questions.explanation: “A good mood” is the natural phrase; “well” and “much” cannot follow “a”.

parts.title: A postcard from Wales
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage:
Dear Mum,
We’re staying [1] a little cottage near the mountains. It’s the best place I’ve ever [2] to. Yesterday we walked [3] a lake and stopped for lunch. The weather was cold, [4] the sun came out in the afternoon. Tomorrow we’re going to visit a castle [5] was built hundreds of years ago. I’ll call you [6] we get back to the city.
Love,
Tom

gaps.explanation: We say we are staying at a cottage.
“The best place I’ve ever been to” uses the present perfect “been”.
We walk around a lake; beside or along would also be possible.
“But” shows contrast between the cold weather and the sun.
“Which” refers to the castle and starts the relative clause.
“I’ll call you when we get back” links two future actions.

parts.title: Part 2: Article or story

options.title: An article for a travel website

parts.title: Short conversations
parts.instructions: Listen to seven short conversations. Choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: andrew
turns.text: Which gate did the app say, Helen? Gate Two?

turns.speaker: helen
turns.text: That’s what it said yesterday. This morning they moved us to Gate Six because of the delay.

turns.speaker: andrew
turns.text: Six is miles away, at the far end of the terminal.

turns.speaker: helen
turns.text: I know, but then the screen updated again. Hold on. Yes, it’s Gate Four now, the one just past the coffee shop.

turns.speaker: andrew
turns.text: Great, that’s close. Shall we get a drink first?

turns.speaker: helen
turns.text: Boarding starts at ten past, so let’s go straight there.

question.explanation: The app showed Gate Two yesterday and then Gate Six, but the screen changed again and Gate Four, past the coffee shop, is the final gate.

turns.speaker: mateo
turns.text: Hello. I need to get to Oxford, please.

turns.speaker: zoe
turns.text: Certainly. Would you like a return? It’s cheaper than two tickets.

turns.speaker: mateo
turns.text: Not today. My friend will drive me back on Sunday. I saw an advert for a group offer, though.

turns.speaker: zoe
turns.text: That’s only for four people or more.

turns.speaker: mateo
turns.text: I’m on my own.

turns.speaker: zoe
turns.text: Then you need a single, which is ten pounds. One way.

turns.speaker: mateo
turns.text: Fine. Can I pay by card? And which platform does it leave from?

turns.speaker: zoe
turns.text: Platform three, in about ten minutes, so you’d better hurry.

question.prompt: What ticket will the traveller buy?
question.explanation: Mateo does not need a return because his friend will drive him back, and the group offer is for four people or more, so he buys a single.

turns.speaker: ruth
turns.text: Here we are at last. I’m glad we walked.

turns.speaker: harry
turns.text: Me too. The guidebook said an hour from the station.

turns.speaker: ruth
turns.text: It must be wrong. We left the station at ten to three, and it’s ten past three now.

turns.speaker: harry
turns.text: Is it? Wow. The taxi driver told us five minutes by car, but I think he was exaggerating.

turns.speaker: ruth
turns.text: Or he drives very fast! Anyway, I’m happy we didn’t hire him.

turns.speaker: harry
turns.text: And it was pretty, along the river.

question.prompt: How long did it take them to reach the castle?
question.explanation: They left at ten to three and arrived at ten past, so the walk took twenty minutes, not the hour in the guidebook or the taxi driver’s five minutes.

turns.speaker: amira
turns.text: Colin, you can’t go to the beach without anything for the sun.

turns.speaker: colin
turns.text: I’ve got sunglasses. I bought them at the airport.

turns.speaker: amira
turns.text: Then you need something else. A towel?

turns.speaker: colin
turns.text: The hotel gives us towels. I’d like something for my head, though. I nearly bought a straw one in the market, but it was too small.

turns.speaker: amira
turns.text: There’s a hat shop across the road with big cotton ones. Five euros.

turns.speaker: colin
turns.text: Perfect. I’ll go now. Wait for me here.

question.explanation: Colin already has sunglasses and the hotel provides towels; he nearly bought something for his head in the market and will now buy a hat across the road.

turns.speaker: freya
turns.text: Which way shall we go to the coast, Paolo? The motorway?

turns.speaker: paolo
turns.text: It’s the quickest, but there’s an accident near junction nine. The radio says it’s closed for hours.

turns.speaker: freya
turns.text: What about the road past the airport?

turns.speaker: paolo
turns.text: That’s normally empty, but they’re working on the bridge. We’d lose time.

turns.speaker: freya
turns.text: Then it’s the old road, the one with the market and the church.

turns.speaker: paolo
turns.text: Slower, but pretty, and we can stop in the village for coffee.

turns.speaker: freya
turns.text: Sounds good.

question.explanation: The motorway is closed after an accident and the airport road has bridge works, so they take the old road and stop in the village.

turns.speaker: dev
turns.text: Excuse me, what time does breakfast finish?

turns.speaker: leah
turns.text: It’s nine o’clock on weekdays, but on Sunday we serve it a bit later.

turns.speaker: dev
turns.text: Until ten?

turns.speaker: leah
turns.text: That was last summer. Now it’s thirty minutes longer, because guests complained that they couldn’t sleep in.

turns.speaker: dev
turns.text: Lovely. And is it the same buffet?

turns.speaker: leah
turns.text: Yes, with hot food until the end. We also have fruit and yoghurt, and I can bring tea to your table if you like.

turns.speaker: dev
turns.text: Then I’ll come down around ten. Thank you very much for your help.

question.prompt: What time does breakfast end on Sunday?
question.explanation: Weekday breakfast ends at nine and last summer’s Sunday time was ten, but now it finishes thirty minutes later, at half past ten.

turns.speaker: gus
turns.text: Hello Anya, welcome back! How was the boat trip you went on with your cousins at the weekend?

turns.speaker: anya
turns.text: Not bad. It was too short, honestly, only an hour, and I’d have liked more time on the island.

turns.speaker: gus
turns.text: And the guide?

turns.speaker: anya
turns.text: Oh, he was great. He answered every question. But it was fifty pounds each.

turns.speaker: gus
turns.text: Fifty! Do you regret it?

turns.speaker: anya
turns.text: Not at all. I saw dolphins, and the children loved it. I’d happily spend the money again next summer.

question.prompt: What did the visitor think of the trip?
question.explanation: Anya says the trip was short and the guide was good; she does not regret the fifty pounds and would spend the money again.

parts.title: Understanding the main idea
parts.instructions: Listen to six short conversations and choose the best answer.

turns.speaker: tobias
turns.text: I’m so glad we left the car at home.

turns.speaker: ingrid
turns.text: Me too. Did you see the cars near the sea? Hundreds, going round and round, and not a single parking space.

turns.speaker: tobias
turns.text: And the ticket was cheap.

turns.speaker: ingrid
turns.text: It was, only eleven pounds each, but I’d have paid double to avoid that.

turns.speaker: tobias
turns.text: Remember last year? We drove around for an hour looking for somewhere to stop.

turns.speaker: ingrid
turns.text: Don’t remind me. And the south end of the beach was shut for cleaning today, but nobody minded, the north end was lovely.

question.prompt: Why are Ingrid and Tobias pleased they took the train?
options: The beach was closed for the day
question.explanation: The ticket was cheap and one end of the beach was shut, but they are pleased mainly because they saw the full roads and remember last year’s search for a place to stop.

turns.speaker: rory
turns.text: That was a good tour, wasn’t it?

turns.speaker: jenny
turns.text: Yes, the guide was excellent. I’d happily go with him again. The old town was lovely too.

turns.speaker: rory
turns.text: We could come back for it next year.

turns.speaker: jenny
turns.text: Maybe. But what I really regret is the museum. We had forty minutes, and they were closing the best rooms as we arrived, the ones with the Roman things.

turns.speaker: rory
turns.text: We can’t change the timetable.

turns.speaker: jenny
turns.text: I know. I just wish we’d had a whole afternoon there.

options: To visit the old town again
To spend longer at the museum
question.explanation: Jenny likes the guide and the old town, but she regrets that the stop at the museum was only forty minutes and wishes it had been a whole afternoon.

turns.speaker: kate
turns.text: So, was the hotel good? You were away for nearly a week.

turns.speaker: frank
turns.text: The bedroom was tiny, but clean. The garden was lovely, though it rained, so we didn’t sit there.

turns.speaker: kate
turns.text: I wanted to sit there too, in the evening. But the food in the morning, wow.

turns.speaker: frank
turns.text: Eggs, fresh bread, the jam they made themselves. They gave us breakfast on a terrace.

turns.speaker: kate
turns.text: That’s what I’ll tell people. Everything else was fine, but that was the star.

question.prompt: What do Kate and Frank agree was the best thing about the hotel?
question.explanation: Frank thinks the room was small and the garden was wet; they both praise the eggs, bread and jam in the morning as the star of the stay.

turns.speaker: dina
turns.text: Oh no, it’s starting to rain. Shall we go back to the hotel and have lunch there?

turns.speaker: wes
turns.text: We’ve only got today. I’d hate to give up.

turns.speaker: dina
turns.text: We could wait in the café until it stops.

turns.speaker: wes
turns.text: The woman said rain in the mountains can last all day. The waterfall is only twenty minutes away, and we’ve got raincoats.

turns.speaker: dina
turns.text: You’re right. It’ll look better with all that water anyway.

turns.speaker: wes
turns.text: Let’s go. We can have lunch at the top, if the kiosk is open.

question.prompt: What do Dina and Wes decide to do?
options: Wait for the rain to stop
question.explanation: Dina suggests going back or waiting in the café, but Wes says rain can last all day and the waterfall is only twenty minutes away, so they walk there.

turns.speaker: mina
turns.text: The board says the 5:10 is delayed by thirty minutes. Oh no, you’ll be late for your meeting.

turns.speaker: vince
turns.text: Honestly, it doesn’t matter. I phoned and they said to start without me.

turns.speaker: mina
turns.text: And aren’t you cross about the announcements? They said it was cancelled first, then platform six, then delayed.

turns.speaker: vince
turns.text: A bit confusing, but the staff were helpful. Actually, I haven’t eaten since breakfast, so now I have time to eat properly. I can get a sandwich.

turns.speaker: mina
turns.text: Good plan. I’ll join you.

question.prompt: How does Vince feel about the delay?
options: Worried that he will miss a meeting
Pleased to have time to eat
question.explanation: Vince has already told the meeting to start without him and finds the staff helpful; he is happy to use the extra time to get a sandwich.

turns.speaker: jess
turns.text: How was the mountain walk, Bram?

turns.speaker: bram
turns.text: The steepest part nearly finished me. I had to stop every ten minutes.

turns.speaker: jess
turns.text: Was it cold?

turns.speaker: bram
turns.text: Freezing at the top, but I had my big coat. And I only took the wrong path once, near the lake. A farmer pointed me back.

turns.speaker: jess
turns.text: So would you do it again?

turns.speaker: bram
turns.text: Definitely. The view from the top was worth every step. I’m so glad I did it.

question.prompt: How does Bram feel about the mountain walk?
options: Glad he did it despite the difficulty
Sorry he went in such cold weather
question.explanation: Bram found the climb hard and cold and took a wrong path once, but he would do it again because the view was worth every step.

parts.title: A talk about a walking holiday
parts.instructions: Listen and complete the notes. Write one or two words, a number, a date or a time in each gap.

turns.speaker: speaker-1
turns.text: Good evening. I’m Claire from Open Road Holidays, and tonight I’m going to tell you about our new walking break. First, the date. We planned to start in May, but the hotel was full, so the holiday begins on the fourteenth of June. The last day is the twentieth. You’ll stay in a small hotel in the village of Penford. Some customers confuse it with Ashby, which is further north, but our hotel is definitely in Penford. It has a garden and a fire in the sitting room. Now, what should you bring? Walking is easy on this holiday, but the paths can be wet and stony. Comfortable boots are important. Trainers aren’t good enough for the hills, so please don’t bring them. You should also pack a coat, because it can rain even in summer. Let me describe the walking itself. On most days, the walks are about eight kilometres, which takes a morning. The longest walk is on the fourth day. It is twelve kilometres, and you finish at the top of Penford Hill. I know that sounds like a lot, but we walk slowly, and there are plenty of stops. Lunch on that day is beside a river. We tried a picnic by the lake, but it was too windy, so the river is the better place, and it has a bridge where you can sit. The group has about twelve people, and a local guide called Ivan will lead us. Ivan has walked these hills for thirty years. Before I finish, remember that the price includes breakfast and dinner. If you have any questions, please come and see me after the talk. Thank you very much for listening.

gaps.prompt: The holiday begins in the month of ___
gaps.explanation: Claire says they planned to start in May, but the hotel was full, so it begins on the fourteenth of June.

gaps.prompt: The hotel is in the village of ___
gaps.explanation: She says some customers confuse it with Ashby, but the hotel is in Penford.

gaps.prompt: For the hills you must have comfortable ___ (not trainers)
gaps.explanation: She says comfortable boots are important and trainers are not good enough.

gaps.prompt: The hardest walk on day four covers ___
gaps.explanation: Most days are about eight kilometres, but the longest walk is twelve kilometres.

gaps.prompt: The day four picnic is next to a ___ (not the lake)
gaps.explanation: A picnic by the lake was too windy, so lunch is beside a river.
She says a local guide called Ivan will lead the group.

parts.title: An interview with a travel writer
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Daniel, you write about travel for a living. Who first encouraged you to write?

turns.speaker: daniel
turns.text: It wasn’t my readers, I didn’t have any then. And my family thought I should find a proper job, although my sister did read my first stories. The person who changed things was my English teacher at school. She told me that my letters from a school trip were better than the essays, and she asked me to write for the school magazine. I think I’d have stopped without her.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Why did you choose a small town for your first trip as a writer?

turns.speaker: daniel
turns.text: Honestly, I had friends in a big city who invited me, but I said no. It wasn’t the only place I could reach either. I wanted to show people that you don’t need a lot of money to enjoy a weekend away. So I chose a quiet town, stayed in a cheap guest house, and the readers liked that it was something they could copy.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Where do you get ideas for places?

turns.speaker: daniel
turns.text: Travel companies send me emails every day, but I almost never use them, they want me to say nice things. Old maps are fun, and I buy them in markets, but they only give me a starting point. The best ideas come from my readers. They write to me about their own villages, and some of those letters are better than any guidebook.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Is there a problem with travelling a lot?

turns.speaker: daniel
turns.text: The food in hotels isn’t always great, but I learned to eat in local cafés. And my luggage has only been lost once, which was an adventure rather than a problem. What really drives me crazy is delays. Trains are late, planes are late, buses don’t arrive, and I can lose half a day. I’ve learned to carry a book for those moments.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: I’ve heard you always carry a notebook. Why is that?

turns.speaker: daniel
turns.text: Well, I do draw a bit, but my maps are terrible, so I don’t draw them for readers. And I write letters on my laptop. The reason is practical. My phone battery often dies after a long day of taking photos, and then I can’t make notes. A small notebook never runs out, so it’s my backup.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: What are you working on now?

turns.speaker: daniel
turns.text: A guide to places you can reach by bus, with no car at all. Mountain holidays are popular, and I’ve done a few, but this book is for people who live in cities and want an easy weekend. It’s difficult, because some timetables are confusing, but I think it will be useful.

questions.prompt: Who first encouraged Daniel to write?
questions.explanation: Daniel says it was not his readers or his family; his English teacher told him his letters were better than his essays and asked him to write for the school magazine.

questions.prompt: Why did he choose a small town for his first trip?
options: To show that trips can be affordable
It was the only place he could visit
questions.explanation: He refused the big city and could have gone elsewhere; he wanted to show that a weekend away does not need much money.

questions.prompt: Where does Daniel get ideas for places?
questions.explanation: Companies and old maps only give him a starting point; the best ideas come from letters that his readers write about their villages.

questions.prompt: What problem does he mention?
questions.explanation: Hotel food and lost luggage are not the problem; what drives him crazy is delays that waste half a day.

questions.prompt: Why does he carry a notebook?
options: He wants to draw maps of each place
He writes long letters to his readers
His phone battery may run out
questions.explanation: He does not draw maps or write letters in it; his phone battery often dies, so the notebook is his backup.

questions.prompt: What is his current writing project about?
questions.explanation: Daniel is writing a guide to places that can be reached by bus; mountain holidays are popular but this book is for easy weekends.

parts.title: Getting to know you
parts.instructions: Answer each question in your own words. Aim to speak for 20–30 seconds.

questions.prompt: Do you enjoy travelling? Tell me about a trip you remember.
What is the best way to travel around your town?
Would you rather visit a city or the countryside? Why?
